newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fidelity to sound out Japanese investors.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity to sound out Japanese investors.

text.p: Fidelity Investments may have come some way from the days when Japanese assumed it sold stereos, but the U.S. mutual fund giant still sees the need to educate Tokyo investors about what it has to offer.
"Japanese people are paying too much for their financial services," said Arthur Jesson, Tokyo office representative for Fidelity Brokerage Services Inc, Fidelity's brokerage arm.
Fidelity will work to bring down fees in Japan through its unique sales methods, he said in an interview.
In addition to direct sales of funds, Jesson said Fidelity is considering holding seminars to educate investors and hopefully lure their money into its financial instruments.
"Education -- people here don't know what mutual funds are. They used to think we sold stereos because of the word 'high fidelity'," he said.

The firm hopes to attract Japanese investors fed up with ultra-low returns by introducing its unique U.S.-style services, Jesson said. "As soon as we get the branch licence we'll be opening up the phones and people will be able to call up and buy our funds."
Although some foreign investment trusts sell their funds directly in Japan, most are sold through the retail networks of Japanese securities houses.
Fidelity aims to beef up sales and cut the costs of its mutual funds by setting up its own brokerage unit, Jesson said.
It has applied to the Finance Ministry for a securities branch licence and expects to be granted one next spring.
It is considering hiring 20 to 30 employees from next spring, but Jesson said it did not have plans to open walk-in branches in the near term.
"We have to be careful of costs," he said, adding that the firm was considering seeking sales by putting advertisements in newspapers and advertising through direct mailing.
"L.L. Bean is a good example. People buy good quality at reasonable prices," he said, referring to the U.S. retailer which sells in Japan mainly through mail-order catalogues.

As well as its financial instruments, Fidelity intends to offer securities brokerage services, a decision that he said was highly influenced by the Japanese authorities' determination to deregulate the Tokyo market.

Although there is no discount brokering in Japan as brokerage commissions are fixed except for large-lot transactions, Jesson said he was keeping open "many options" pending deregulation. Fidelity engages heavily in discount brokering in the United States.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has included a call to end fixed commissions in his five-year "Big Bang" plan to liberalise Tokyo financial markets.
"We support the prime minister 100 percent," Jesson said, adding that there was a new mood at the Finance Ministry.

Fidelity had given up applying for a securities licence in Japan in the past, but had decided to go through with it now as there was a feeling that "this time they're going to do it", he said, referring to deregulation.
Jesson said Fidelity did not intend to sell the same funds it offered in the United States, such as the Magellan fund, as they would not be tax-efficient in Japan.

A mutual fund is a fund operated by an investment company that pools together money from many investors to establish a diversified portfolio. Investors receive dividends in proportion to their holdings.
